source.title: Why LoRA Resists Label Noise: A Theoretical Framework for Noise-Robust Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some figure values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and tests LoRA’s resistance to label noise, qualifying the broad memorization claim with rank-dependent limits and temporal separation. Its setting is low-rank fine-tuning, not the original standard-network setting.
record.gate_note: The paper’s comparisons to results cited from Biderman et al., Liu et al., and other prior work are not this study’s results. RACT’s noise-detection performance alone does not measure the claim versions; included rows focus on rank-dependent training accuracy, test accuracy under varying noise, and clean/noisy training dynamics.
record.test_reason: The study measures fitting corrupted training labels and clean-versus-noisy learning dynamics in a new setting: low-rank fine-tuning. These results bear on V4 and V6. It does not test V1's completely random labeling in standard network training.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors propose a rank-dependent, existential capacity restriction, an optimal-rank tradeoff, and earlier clean-pattern learning than noise memorization. They report qualitative empirical validation and present RACT primarily as a noise-detection method with competitive classification accuracy. Their results do not establish universal inability of low-rank adapters to memorize noisy classifications.
record.recipe_differences: Uses low-rank fine-tuning of pretrained models, symmetric label-noise injection, rank sweeps, and theoretical capacity analysis; does not reproduce the original full-network random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Rank and noise rate change training accuracy and memorization behavior; the reported temporal dynamics are for rank 8 and 30% noise.

fits_no_version.finding: An existential rank-dependent capacity bound for arbitrary output assignments, with a qualified classification interpretation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-rank updates can leave some target assignments unrealizable when sample constraints exceed their effective dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: RACT maintains approximately 91% AG News classification accuracy across 20–40% label corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rank-based noise detection and sample selection can maintain classification performance under moderate symmetric label noise.

record.problems: The paper states that its capacity bound is existential and asymptotic, its temporal-separation theorem uses a linearized regime, and the exact bias-variance decomposition is for squared loss. Experiments cover medium-scale datasets; some results are single-seed, and Appendix A reports figure-based accuracy trends without per-condition numerical values.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, chance-level test performance, and fitting with unchanged standard-network architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios for true versus random labels and convergence slowdown across corruption fractions. RACT's two-adapter overhead does not test these.

The full corruption range through completely random labels and a paired training/test-error trajectory showing steady degradation toward chance. Reported training fits cover selected corruption rates.
Regularization ablations testing random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
A comparison between entirely random and entirely real label datasets; empirical evidence here concerns clean and corrupted subsets during LoRA fine-tuning.

missing.what: The authors report that larger ranks shorten the delay before noise memorization. This is an additional empirical condition dependence of V6, omitted from R7.

Theoretical temporal separation under linearized gradient flow: primarily clean learning before t*/2 and noisy fitting after 2t*, assuming separated clean-gradient singular values. Record separately from the empirical loss trajectory.

record.verdict_notes: LoRA rank restrictions qualify the extension to fine-tuning; they do not contradict V1's stated standard-network experiment. Comparisons with full fine-tuning are attributed to prior work, with comprehensive direct comparisons deferred.

versions.untested_parts: Tests LoRA under symmetric label corruption and gives a theoretical bound for arbitrary label assignments; does not test standard deep networks with the original architecture and optimizer, fully random labels, or test error at chance.
No comparison of time to fit true versus random labels or convergence time by corruption fraction.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Does not report training and test error across the full range from clean to fully random labels for the same unchanged model; empirical rank sweep covers selected noise rates.
Weight decay and LoRA dropout are set in experiments, but not ablated to test fitting random labels or true-label generalization.
Tests clean versus synthetically corrupted labels in LoRA, including a stated temporal sequence; does not compare fully random labels with true labels in the original standard-network setting.

rows.subject: rank-r LoRA
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 3.3 bounds whether rank-r updates can memorize arbitrary label assignments.
rows.measure: Existence of label assignments that cannot be memorized
rows.value: Some label assignments cannot be achieved by any rank-r update.
rows.note: An existential capacity result: it does not establish that every assignment below the bound is learnable or report a training run.
rows.check: An existential bound on achieving arbitrary outputs does not measure fitting randomly corrupted class labels or degradation with corruption rate. The paper explicitly qualifies its classification interpretation; the theorem should remain a theoretical finding rather than an empirical effect row.

rows.subject: LoRA adapters, ranks r=2 and r=4
rows.operation_detail: Trained on AG News with synthetic symmetric label noise; final training accuracy measured after convergence.
rows.baseline: At 0% noise, all ranks achieve near-perfect training accuracy (> 99%).
rows.value: At higher noise rates, low-rank adapters (r=2, 4) show training accuracy capped below 100%.
rows.note: The text does not give separate numeric accuracy values for each of these ranks and noise rates.
rows.check: Supports incomplete fitting at low ranks under higher corruption. Remove V1: no completely random labeling is tested. Separate rank/noise conditions when figure values are available; the text does not establish the same deficit at every nonzero noise rate.

rows.subject: LoRA adapters, ranks r=32 and r=64
rows.operation_detail: Trained on AG News with synthetic symmetric label noise; final training accuracy measured after convergence.
rows.value: High-rank adapters (r=32, 64) can approach 100% training accuracy even at 40% noise.
rows.note: The result is described jointly for the two ranks; no separate values are stated.
rows.check: Near-perfect training fit is reported for ranks 32 and 64 at 40% noise. This bears on V4's fitting component, without measuring its test-error trajectory. Remove V1 because labels are only partly corrupted.

source_check.correct: At 0% noise, all ranks, including 32 and 64, achieve training accuracy above 99%.
source_check.problem: The baseline is marked not stated, but the text supplies a clean-label baseline for all ranks.

rows.subject: RACT
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated classification accuracy as symmetric label-noise rate varied.
rows.note: Table 3 reports single-seed results except the 30% row, which includes ±0.3.
rows.check: RACT's classification accuracy measures the proposed noise-mitigation method's performance. Sample selection and optional retraining prevent interpreting it as V4's joint memorization/generalization trajectory.

rows.subject: RACT
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated classification accuracy as symmetric label-noise rate varied.
rows.note: The table specifies a single seed for the noise-rate comparison; the paper separately reports this accuracy across three seeds in Section 5.2.
rows.check: Method-performance result, not a V4 effect row. Table 3 says single seed but repeats the multi-seed 30% result; retain this reporting inconsistency.

rows.subject: RACT
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated classification accuracy as symmetric label-noise rate varied.
rows.note: Table 3 reports single-seed results except the 30% row, which includes ±0.3; no chance-level comparison is given.
rows.check: Method-performance result without corresponding training fit on the original corrupted dataset; it cannot establish V4.

rows.subject: LoRA (r=8)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked loss separately on samples with clean original labels and samples with corrupted labels during training.
rows.measure: Training loss by clean versus noisy sample group over epochs
rows.value: Clean-sample loss decreases rapidly in early epochs; noisy-sample loss initially plateaus, then decreases as the model begins memorizing noise.
rows.note: The text states the sequence but provides no numerical loss values.
rows.check: The stated loss sequence directly supports clean patterns being learned before corrupted labels. Evidence is qualitative; separate numerical losses are unavailable.
